description:
In the depths of the Great Depression, thousands of men came to a remote desert gorge on the Colorado River, about 30 miles from a small railroad town called Las Vegas. Their job was to build the largest dam the world had ever seen.

This documentary tells the story of Hoover Dam, built in Black Canyon on the border of Nevada and Arizona between 1931 and 1936. We follow the Six Companies consortium and its superintendent, Frank Crowe, as crews blasted four giant diversion tunnels to move the river out of the way. We meet the high scalers who swung on ropes high above the canyon floor to pry loose rock from the walls, and we see how engineers poured about 3.25 million cubic yards of concrete in interlocking blocks, cooled by pipes carrying chilled water.

Over the life of the project about 21,000 people worked on the dam, and 112 deaths are commonly associated with its construction. The finished dam stands 726 feet tall, it was completed about two years ahead of schedule, and the lake behind it, Lake Mead, is the largest reservoir in the United States by capacity when full.

Figures are drawn from the Bureau of Reclamation and widely published histories of the dam.
